- Exam 1 is Thursday in class; tonight's recitation is exam preparation. The third assignment is released on Thursday

- Last lecture stopped after shortcut learning. These are the slides it did not reach: it showed when a fit fails to carry over to new data, and these say what to do about it - Regularization is the umbrella term. The next slides show three kinds: a penalty on the weights (also called weight decay or L2 regularization), dropout, and more examples, real or made by altering the ones you have. Early stopping, from the learning curves, is a fourth - Then the weight penalty applied to a model of a neuron, ridge regression, which the second assignment used and the next assignment uses again

- Conventions differ by a factor of 2. PyTorch's weight_decay and the demo use (λ/2)‖w‖², and scikit-learn's LogisticRegression uses C = 1/λ on the summed loss. When you choose λ on validation data, only its order of magnitude matters - The polynomial fit is a linear regression on the powers of x (x, x², …, x⁹), fit by least squares. With the penalty added, it is ridge regression, the method the next slides apply to a model of a neuron and the assignments use as RidgeCV - Test RMSE falls from 0.86 without the penalty to 0.34 with λ = 10⁻⁷ or 10⁻³, and rises to 0.61 with λ = 1 - The polynomial with 10 coefficients and 10 points, from last lecture. Without a penalty the coefficients reach about a million in size; with λ = 10⁻³, about 17 - Large coefficients are what let the curve swing between the points. Keeping them small keeps the curve smooth - w is the weight vector: in the polynomial, all 10 coefficients, the constant term included, and the penalty covers every one of them. For a network the same penalty runs over every weight. λ is the strength of the penalty, a hyperparameter (elsewhere in the course λ is an eigenvalue). Choose λ on validation data, never on the test set - The second assignment added this penalty to a readout (weight_decay); the next assignment chooses its strength on validation data - scikit-learn's LogisticRegression adds this penalty by default. A PyTorch loop does not, unless you pass weight_decay to the optimizer; PyTorch then applies it to every parameter it is given, biases included - Bishop (2006), Fig. 1.7, shows the same effect

- The weight penalty of the previous slides, applied to a model of a neuron instead of a curve - What is the same and what is new between the two assignments. Second assignment: one IT site from Bao et al. (2020), features from one layer of a network, nested cross-validation, scored by R². Next assignment: electrodes in V1, V4 and IT from the THINGS Ventral Stream Spiking Dataset (two monkeys, photographs), features from each of ResNet-50's 16 blocks, the same StandardScaler + RidgeCV with one λ per electrode, scored by the noise-corrected correlation (Pearson r divided by the square root of the electrode's reliability), and the question is which block predicts which area best. Same tool, three areas, sixteen stages - An encoding model predicts a neuron's response to each image from a network's features. With the penalty λ‖w‖² added to the squared error, the fit is called ridge regression. It is scored by R² on held-out images - The target is one IT site's response to each of the 1,224 object images of Bao et al. (2020); the features are the 512 units of the trained ResNet-18's late layer. A random fifth of the images is held out and never seen by the fit - The model is a weighted sum of the features plus a bias, fit by least squares: linear regression. Run with a small enough step on a continuous target, the delta rule minimizes the same squared error - λ is chosen by leave-one-out cross-validation within the 980 training images (scikit-learn's RidgeCV). The held-out fifth only scores the chosen fit. The held-out curve on the right is drawn to show what the penalty does; it was not used to choose λ - R² = 1 − (squared error of the prediction) / (squared error of predicting the mean response). 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than the mean, and it can be negative. The baselines lecture used the squared correlation, which is close for a good fit - Right panel: with almost no penalty, 512 weights fit the training images closely (R² 0.85) and predict held-out images poorly (0.28): overfitting. As λ grows, the training fit gets worse and the held-out fit better, up to a point (0.69) - The second assignment fit this model with nested cross-validation: λ is chosen inside each training fold, and the held-out R² comes from the outer folds - The same model, the same `RidgeCV`, twice. In the second assignment the target was one IT site and the features one network layer; in the next, the targets are recording sites in three areas and the features come from each of 16 stages of a network, so the fit is repeated 16 times per site - One λ per site: each site gets its own penalty, chosen on its own training images. RidgeCV does this with alpha_per_target=True - Nested cross-validation keeps the two decisions apart: λ is chosen on training folds; the score comes from images that were not used to choose anything

- Dropout (Srivastava et al. 2014): each hidden unit is switched off with probability p (often one half) at every training step, a different random set each time. A unit cannot count on any particular other unit, so the network cannot build fragile combinations that fit single training images. At test time all units are on, with their outputs scaled so their average matches training. PyTorch does the scaling during training instead (kept units × 1/(1−p)), so in evaluation mode nothing is rescaled. AlexNet used dropout in its fully connected layers; without it, Krizhevsky et al. (2012) wrote, the network "exhibits substantial overfitting" - L1 penalizes the sum of the absolute values of the weights instead of their squares. It drives many weights to exactly zero, so the model uses fewer inputs - The penalties differ in detail, but they share one effect: they restrict which weight settings training can reach, so the network has fewer ways to fit the noise in its training data - In PyTorch: nn.Dropout(p=0.5) as a layer; model.train() switches it on and model.eval() switches it off. Weight decay is the weight_decay argument of the optimizer

- Last lecture: the same **degree-9 polynomial** fitted to 10, 15, 30 and 100 points; test RMSE 0.86 → 0.31 - With 10 points it passes through every one; with 100 it cannot, and follows the curve instead - <mark>More examples always help the same model</mark>: overfitting is flexibility relative to the number of examples; $\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert$ falls from a million to 8,700 with no penalty at all - The slide from last lecture: the model is kept and data is added. Error on new points 0.86 with N = 10, 0.34 with 15, 0.35 with 30, 0.31 with 100. Training error rises from 0.00 to 0.28, toward the noise level of 0.30: with many points the curve can no longer fit the noise - A network's flexibility is harder to count than 10 coefficients, but the same trade holds: more training images make the same network overfit less. More labelled data is the most reliable fix for overfitting, when it can be had

- Labelled data is expensive, so the next best thing to more data is to make more from what you have - Each epoch shows a different random version of each image, which makes memorizing the training images harder - Flips that would change the label (a 6 and a 9, a b and a d) must be left out. Speech recognizers train on recordings with stretches of time and bands of frequency masked out (SpecAugment, Park et al. 2019); medical-image networks on rotated and re-lit scans - Krizhevsky et al. (2012) trained AlexNet on random 224 × 224 crops of each 256 × 256 photo and their mirror images, which multiplies the training set by 2,048, plus colour changes - Photograph: THINGSplus, public domain (CC0)

- torchvision.transforms.Compose applies the list in order to each image as it is loaded; the random transforms draw new parameters every time, so the training set is effectively unbounded. The held-out and test loaders use only Resize, CenterCrop, ToTensor and Normalize - Krizhevsky et al. (2012) used random 224 × 224 crops of each 256 × 256 photo and their mirror images, which multiplies the training set by 2,048, plus colour changes. The next assignment's fine-tuning uses a pipeline like this one - Augmentations that change the label must be left out: a flip turns a b into a d and a 6 into a 9. Speech recognizers mask stretches of time and frequency (SpecAugment); medical-image networks rotate and re-light scans

- The networks of the last three lectures connected every unit to every input. For images that is wasteful, and it misses something: an object can appear anywhere. The next slides turn the dense layer into a convolution, the operation every vision network since has used

- Left: a two-layer perceptron over a 6 × 6 image: every pixel to every hidden unit (216 weights, all different), every hidden unit to every output. Right: a convolutional layer: each hidden unit reads a 3 × 3 patch, and the nine weights (colour-coded) are the same for every unit, so the layer has nine weights instead of 216 and detects the same feature wherever it appears. A second convolutional layer reads patches of the map in the same way - Local connections and shared weights are the two changes that turn the perceptron into a convolutional network; the next slide counts what that saves, and the ones after show it as one operation, the convolution

- Counts are weights only, without biases. The image size is the 224 × 224 × 3 input stated in Krizhevsky et al. (2012) - A dense (fully connected) layer is the MLP layer of the lecture on learning the weights: every unit has one weight for every input value - Reusing a filter is called weight sharing (also parameter sharing): the 96 filters are the only first-layer weights, however many positions they are applied at - A dense unit could learn a local pattern, but it would have to learn it separately at every position, from many more examples

- Retinotopic organization: neighbouring points of the visual field are handled by neighbouring cells, so cortex holds a map of the image, with the same local machinery everywhere - On a computer the same answer comes from one filter applied at every position in turn, so the weights exist once: weight sharing. Counts are weights only, without biases, for the 224 × 224 × 3 input of Krizhevsky et al. (2012): 96 × 11 × 11 × 3 = 34,848, against 96 × 150,528 = 14,450,688 for dense units - Both the template and each window have their mean removed and are scaled to unit length, so the dot product is a cosine: 1.00 at the position the template was cut from, lower elsewhere. The template-matching idea is the model neuron's: among inputs of the same length, wᵀx is largest for the input that looks like w

- The window's patch has its mean subtracted before the dot product, so the filter reports contrast, not brightness; ReLU sets negative values to 0 in the map - Vertical stripes light up the tiger's flank; horizontal stripes light up the water's edge; the centre–surround filter marks spots and edges of any orientation - The map has 90 × 90 positions, the image 96 × 96: no padding, stride 1, as the next slides define - The demo is on the course site with the other demos

- Computed here: the tiger (grey levels, 224 × 224) correlated with one 11 × 11 Gabor filter at stride 1 and zero padding 5 (both defined on the stride-and-padding slide), then a ReLU. The circle marks the largest value of the map, at the boxed image position. This oriented filter responds along the tiger's stripes that share its angle - Each value of the map is one unit's response; all the units of one map share the filter's weights - Equivariance: the map moves when the image moves. Invariance: the output does not change at all. Pooling adds invariance, a few slides on - PyTorch's Conv2d computes this sliding dot product without flipping the filter, which mathematicians call cross-correlation; deep-learning papers call it convolution all the same

- One filter slid over the image gives one feature map. A layer has many filters, and their maps stack into a volume: height × width × channels, one channel per filter. The next layer's filters then read all channels at once, which is why their weights have a depth of C_{l−1} in the notation that follows - Computed here: four Gabor filters at 0°, 45°, 90°, 135° on the tiger in grey levels; each map lights up where the stripes of the image run along that filter's orientation

- The input image is the first stack, A^[0], with three channels (red, green, blue) - One filter spans every input channel: a first-layer filter on a colour image is k × k × 3; a filter in a layer whose input has 64 channels is k × k × 64. Each filter makes one output channel - Per element: A^[l] at row i, column j, channel c is g of (the sum over the filter's rows u, columns v and input channels c′ of K at u, v, c′, c times A^[l−1] at i+u, j+v, c′, plus b_c) - W^sp is the spatial width; the superscript keeps it apart from the weight matrix W - In PyTorch, nn.Conv2d(C_in, C_out, kernel_size=k) stores the filters as a tensor of shape (C_out, C_in, k, k)

- ⌊ ⌋ rounds down to a whole number - Padding that keeps the size unchanged at stride 1 (p = (k − 1)/2 for odd k) is often called "same"; no padding is "valid" - Downsampling, by stride or by pooling, makes each unit of a later layer depend on a larger region of the image: its receptive field grows, as it does from V1 to IT - In PyTorch: nn.Conv2d(3, 64, kernel_size=7, stride=2, padding=3) is ResNet-50's first layer

- The numbers are a schematic example, not a recording - Two ways to shrink a map: pooling, or a stride-2 convolution; many modern networks use mostly the second, then one global average. Lin, Chen & Yan (2014), Network in Network, introduced global average pooling in place of large dense layers at the top of a network - In PyTorch: nn.MaxPool2d(2) for max-pooling; nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1) averages each channel down to a single value - Pooling has no weights to learn

- From here on, the brain: the behavior to explain, the areas from the retina to IT, and Hubel and Wiesel's cells, which turn out to compute the two operations of the convolutional network, a weighted sum and a pooling - V1 sees edges in small patches; people recognize whole objects in a glance. The rest of today asks what happens between the two, in the brain and in a network - The brain half follows the ventral stream: center–surround cells, then V1's simple and complex cells, then the areas above V1. On the way it asks a question about learning: V1's oriented receptive fields can be learned from natural images alone, with no labels, by a sparse code - The network half prepares the next assignment: convolution, pooling, residual networks, BatchNorm, and reusing a pretrained network

- Core object recognition: naming the object in a single glance, across changes in position, size and background (DiCarlo, Zoccolan & Rust 2012) - The movie: ten photographs from the animal / non-animal set of Serre, Oliva & Poggio (2007), five animals and five distractors at the four viewing distances; each is shown for two frames at 30 frames per second, about 67 ms, after a fixation cross, then a two-second window to answer, then the answer - Thorpe, Fize & Marlot (1996): photographs flashed for 20 ms, a go/no-go response to animals; 94% correct. The EEG over frontal cortex differed between animal and non-animal trials from about 150 ms after the image - Too fast for eye movements or many back-and-forth loops: recognition rides mostly on one feedforward sweep through the visual system. Feedback connections exist everywhere; the speed limits how much they can contribute to the first answer

- Cauchoix, Crouzet, Fize & Serre (2016): two monkeys trained on the rapid animal / non-animal task with the same photographs people see; intracranial electrodes over intermediate and higher ventral areas (V4, posterior IT). A linear readout of the recorded activity reported the category early enough to drive the behavioural response, and the images the readout got wrong were the ones the monkeys got wrong - The movie: one monkey at the screen, photographs flashed one after another, responses at the box

- The figure is DiCarlo, Zoccolan & Rust (2012), Fig. 1: the macaque ventral stream (A) and its areas stacked with their typical latencies and approximate neuron counts (B). AIT, CIT, PIT: anterior, central and posterior IT - LGN: lateral geniculate nucleus, the relay between retina and V1. IT: inferior temporal cortex - Hung, Kreiman, Poggio & DiCarlo (2005): about 100 IT neurons, over windows as short as 12.5 ms, carried enough information for a linear classifier to report object identity and category, and the readout generalized over positions and sizes - The geometry lecture called this untangling (DiCarlo & Cox 2007): in pixels two objects' images cannot be separated by a flat (linear) boundary; in IT they can - The question for the rest of the lecture: what operation, repeated, gets from edges to objects?

- Kuffler (1953) recorded retinal ganglion cells of the cat with small spots of light: an on-centre cell fires to light in a small central region and is suppressed by light in the ring around it; off-centre cells do the opposite. LGN cells, one synapse on, have the same organization - Because centre and surround cancel, a uniform field does nothing and an edge or a spot does: the retina already computes contrast. These are the inputs Hubel and Wiesel's cortical cells are built from, on the next slides

- The original Hubel and Wiesel film, shown in the first lecture: the experimenter moves a projected bar over the screen while the recorded neuron's spikes are played as clicks. The cell is silent for most positions and orientations and fires briskly for one - Torsten Wiesel describes the experiments at iBiology (linked in the demo page)

- Hubel and Wiesel (1962) mapped receptive fields in cat visual cortex with spots and bars projected on a screen, marking by hand where light excited the cell (triangles) and where it inhibited it (crosses). Circular maps (a, b) are the centre–surround cells of the LGN and layer 4; the elongated ones (c–g) are simple cells, selective for the orientation of a bar - The schematic on the right is the textbook summary of such maps: an ON stripe between OFF flanks (or the reverse), one orientation per cell. A Gabor function, a grating inside a Gaussian window, fits these maps with a few numbers (orientation, stripe width, phase, window size; Jones and Palmer 1987); the second assignment fit Gabors to network units the same way - The cell's response falls off smoothly as a bar is rotated away from its preferred orientation: its orientation tuning curve, typically 20–40° wide at half height

- Kobatake and Tanaka (1994) found each IT cell's "critical feature" by reducing a photograph of an object step by step to the simplest shape that still drove the cell; Tanaka (1996) collected typical critical features by area - Desimone et al. (1984): a face-selective IT neuron responds to faces and cartoons of faces, not to scrambled parts or to a hand; contrast reversal and removing colour hardly matter, removing the eyes does - Tolerance grows with selectivity: IT cells keep responding to their preferred object across changes of position, size and, within limits, view; this is the invariance side of the hierarchy

- Tanaka's table is from 1996. Since then: Pasupathy and Connor (2001) parameterized V4 tuning with a family of curved shapes (curvature and angular position); Freeman, Ziemba, Heeger, Simoncelli and Movshon (2013) found V2, not V1, selective for naturalistic texture statistics; the Gallant lab (Kay et al. 2008) fit V1 from thousands of natural photographs and later natural movies, the start of encoding models on natural images - The current standard: the THINGS images, 1,854 object concepts photographed; TVSD (Papale et al. 2025) recorded V1, V4 and IT of two monkeys to 22,248 of them, the dataset the next assignment uses. The same images have human fMRI, MEG and behaviour (THINGS-data), so one stimulus set now runs across species and methods

- Receptive field: the part of the visual field a neuron responds to. Kobatake and Tanaka (1994) mapped them along the ventral stream of the macaque, from V2 to anterior IT: each square is one cell's field, drawn where it sits in the visual field, with a line to the recording site - Fields grow with each area, roughly doubling from V1 to V2 and again to V4, and latency grows with them: V1 responds near 40 ms after an image, IT near 100 ms - The previous slide showed what the cells of each area prefer

- Hung et al. (2005): spike counts from about 300 IT sites in a 100-ms window; a linear classifier (the course's readout, a weighted sum of the sites) identified the object's category, and its identity, from the first 100 ms of response, and generalized to positions and sizes it was not trained on - A small population suffices: performance rises quickly with the number of sites and saturates. This is the empirical fact behind "a linear readout of IT" throughout the course

- Hubel and Wiesel's proposal, still the textbook model: several LGN cells whose centres lie in a row converge on one cortical cell; a bar of light along the row drives all of them at once, so the cortical cell fires strongly. Tilt the bar and it crosses fewer centres and more inhibitory surrounds, so the input drops; the cortical cell, which needs most of its inputs active, stops first - Computed on model cells: each LGN rate is the bar's overlap with a centre-surround kernel, rectified; the simple cell fires when the sum of its four inputs exceeds a threshold. Frames at 0°, 15°, 30°, 60°, 90°; the simple cell's rate is 1.00, 0.14, 0, 0, 0 - The weighted-sum neuron of the first lectures is this cell: the LGN cells are its inputs, the convergence its weights

- Hubel and Wiesel's proposal, still the textbook model: several LGN cells whose centres lie in a row converge on one cortical cell; a bar of light along the row drives all of them at once, so the cortical cell fires strongly. Tilt the bar and it crosses fewer centres and more inhibitory surrounds, so the input drops; the cortical cell, which needs most of its inputs active, stops first - Computed on model cells: each LGN rate is the bar's overlap with a centre-surround kernel, rectified; the simple cell fires when the sum of its four inputs exceeds a threshold. Frames at 0°, 15°, 30°, 60°, 90°; the simple cell's rate is 1.00, 0.14, 0, 0, 0 - The weighted-sum neuron of the first lectures is this cell: the LGN cells are its inputs, the convergence its weights

Frames at 0°, 15°, 30°, 60°, 90°; the simple cell's rate is 1.00, 0.14, 0, 0, 0 - The weighted-sum neuron of the first lectures is this cell: the LGN cells are its inputs, the convergence its weights

- Hubel and Wiesel's second wiring proposal: a complex cell pools several simple cells of the same orientation whose fields lie side by side, so it keeps the orientation selectivity and loses the position selectivity. A bar of the right orientation drives it wherever it falls within the pooled fields - Computed on model cells: each simple cell's response is a Gaussian in the bar's position (width 0.5, fields one unit apart, so neighbours overlap); the complex cell sums the three and saturates at 1. Its response stays high across all three fields, where each simple cell covers only its own - Two steps: a weighted sum builds selectivity (the simple cell), pooling builds tolerance (the complex cell). The rest of today repeats this pair up the hierarchy and into networks

- The summary of V1's organization as Hubel and Wiesel drew it: centre–surround inputs, simple cells, complex cells - Convolution is the weighted sum replicated at every position; max-pooling is the complex cell; the Neocognitron and HMAX repeat the pair, next

- The next slides follow the idea of the last few slides, selectivity then invariance, through the decades before deep learning: Fukushima's Neocognitron and HMAX, the models that train end to end - Convolution and pooling are introduced on the way, where they first appeared

- Fukushima built the Neocognitron directly from Hubel and Wiesel's two cell types: a plane of S-cells all sharing one template, and C-cells that pool over a neighbourhood of S-cells in that plane. Stacking the pair gives position tolerance that grows with depth - It recognized handwritten digits whatever their position and with some distortion, in 1980, with unsupervised learning (a Hebbian rule that reinforced the strongest responses) and no backpropagation - The figure is the paper's Fig. 2: the cell planes and how each cell reads a small patch of the layer below; the paper's Fig. 1 maps Hubel and Wiesel's cell types onto these layers

- The figure is the model half of Serre, Oliva & Poggio (2007), Fig. 1: solid circles are simple units (tuning), dashed circles complex units (MAX); the table beside it gives each layer's receptive-field size in degrees and its number of units - HMAX's S1 units are Gabor filters at several scales; the max over position and scale gives C1; S2 units are tuned to patches of C1 responses sampled from natural images, without labels; the only part trained on labels is the readout at the top - The point of the exercise was the constraint: receptive-field sizes, layer by layer, the tuning widths and the pooling were taken from recordings, so the model could be tested against data it was not fit to. The next slide is that test - I built this model during my PhD with Tomaso Poggio

- The table is from Serre and Poggio (2010), Communications of the ACM, with its own colour code: black for data used to derive the parameters, red for data consistent with the model but not used to fit it, blue for correct predictions - The V4 MAX prediction (Riesenhuber and Poggio 1999) was tested by Gawne and Martin (2002); the V1 complex-cell MAX by Lampl, Ferster, Poggio and Riesenhuber (2004). Cadieu et al. (2007) fit the model's S2 units to Pasupathy and Connor's V4 cells tuned to curved boundaries - Hung et al. (2005): a linear readout of about 300 IT neurons reports object category 100 ms after the image appears; the same readout works on the model's top units - The lesson is not that HMAX was right in every detail; it is that a model whose parts are constrained by data can be wrong in ways you can find

- d′ (d-prime) measures how well observers separate animal from non-animal images, correcting for how often they say "animal" overall; 0 is chance - The four distances go from a close-up of the head to a small animal in a wide scene; each animal image has a distractor scene matched for its statistics. Model (red) and observers (blue) agree across all four, and the images one finds hard the other tends to find hard too - The mask, shown 80 ms after the image, limits the time for feedback from higher areas, which is what makes the task a test of the feedforward sweep - Rapid categorization is the simplest piece of vision, not a representative one: attention, grouping and eye movements return when there is time, and so does feedback; a later lecture takes that up

- Today: regularization, the move from the perceptron to the convolutional network, the visual system it was modelled on, and the models built from that biology before deep learning - Next lecture starts with the slides held over from today: the mini-HMAX you will train, how ResNet-50 is made deep (residual blocks, BatchNorm), how to reuse a trained network, what a trained network learns, and how scale took over from models like HMAX. Then explainability

- Yamins, Hong, Cadieu, Solomon, Seibert & DiCarlo (2014), Performance-optimized hierarchical models predict neural responses in higher visual cortex - Zhuang, Yan, Nayebi, Schrimpf, Frank, DiCarlo & Yamins (2021), Unsupervised neural network models of the ventral visual stream - Konkle & Alvarez (2022), A self-supervised domain-general learning framework for human ventral stream representation - Kar, Kubilius, Schmidt, Issa & DiCarlo (2019), Evidence that recurrent circuits are critical to the ventral stream's execution of core object recognition behavior - Jinsi, Henderson & Tarr (2023), Early experience with low-pass filtered images facilitates visual category learning in a neural network model - Lu, Thorat, Cichy & Kietzmann (2026), Adopting a human developmental visual diet yields robust and shape-based AI vision - Also cited today and worth reading: Kuffler (1953) and Hubel & Wiesel (1962) on receptive fields, Fukushima (1980) on the Neocognitron, Serre, Oliva & Poggio (2007) on rapid categorization - Before posting, skim the existing entries on your paper; your post must add something not already said
